pumac-2009-team-01.title: Find the number
pumac-2009-team-01.body:
Take $p=3$: $1+3+9+27+81=121=11^2$, and $121=5!+1$. So $n=121$ satisfies both descriptions, and since the problem states that the square is unique, $n=121$.

(Why $5!+1$: the numbers $k!+1$ with three digits are only $5!+1=121$ and $6!+1=721$, and $721$ is not a square.)

**Answer: 121**

pumac-2009-team-02.title: Count how often each term occurs
pumac-2009-team-02.body:
In $a_1^2+\cdots+a_{96}^2$ the term $\frac1{n^2}$ occurs in $a_1^2,\ldots,a_n^2$, i.e. $n$ times, and a cross term $\frac{2}{mn}$ ($m<n$) occurs in $a_1^2,\ldots,a_m^2$, i.e. $m$ times. So $$\sum_{k=1}^{96}a_k^2=\sum_{n=1}^{96}\frac{n}{n^2}+\sum_{n=1}^{96}\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\frac{2m}{mn}=\sum_{n=1}^{96}\frac1n+\sum_{n=1}^{96}\frac{2(n-1)}{n}=\sum_{n=1}^{96}\frac{2n-1}{n}.$$ Adding $a_1=\sum\frac1n$: $$a_1+\sum a_k^2=\sum_{n=1}^{96}\frac{2n}{n}=2\cdot96=192.$$

**Answer: 192**

pumac-2009-team-03.title: Count the choices
pumac-2009-team-03.body:
Let $M=\{a,b,c,d\}$. The relation determines $f(A)=\bigcup_{x\in A}f(\{x\})$ for non-empty $A$ from the four values $f(\{a\}),\ldots,f(\{d\})$. Taking $B=\varnothing$ gives $f(A)\cup f(\varnothing)=f(A)$, so $f(\varnothing)\subseteq f(\{x\})$ for each $x$. Conversely, any choice of $S=f(\varnothing)$ and sets $f(\{x\})\supseteq S$ gives a valid $f$.

If $|S|=j$ there are $\binom4j$ choices of $S$, and each $f(\{x\})$ is $S$ together with any subset of the other $4-j$ elements: $2^{4-j}$ choices, so $(2^{4-j})^4$ for the four singletons. Total $$\sum_{j=0}^4\binom4j16^{4-j}=(16+1)^4=17^4=83521.$$

**Answer: 83521**

pumac-2009-team-04.title: Ptolemy and similar triangles
pumac-2009-team-04.body:
$P$ lies on arc $BC$. By Ptolemy in $ABPC$: $PA\cdot BC=AB\cdot PC+AC\cdot PB=BC(PB+PC)$, so $PA=PB+PC=275$.

Triangles $PBD$ and $PAC$ are similar: $\angle BPD=\angle APC=\angle ABC=60^\circ$ and $\angle PBD=\angle PBC=\angle PAC$ (same arc $PC$). So $\frac{PB}{PA}=\frac{PD}{PC}$, giving $PD=\frac{55\cdot220}{275}=44$. Then $AD=PA-PD=275-44=231$.

**Answer: 231**

pumac-2009-team-05.title: Guess and prove by induction
pumac-2009-team-05.body:
From (2) with $y=0$: $(x+1)+x\mathbin{\S}1=3x$, so $x\mathbin{\S}1=2x-1$. This suggests $x\mathbin{\S}y=xy+x-y$, which holds for $y=0$ and $y=1$. Suppose it holds for $y$ and all $x$. Then rule (2) determines $x\mathbin{\S}(y+1)$: $$x\mathbin{\S}(y+1)=3(xy+x-y)-xy+2y-\big((x+1)y+(x+1)-y\big)=xy+2x-y-1=x(y+1)+x-(y+1),$$ so the formula holds for $y+1$. Hence $x\mathbin{\S}y=xy+x-y$ for all $y\ge0$.

$178\mathbin{\S}255=178\cdot255+178-255=45390-77=45313$.

**Answer: 45313**

pumac-2009-team-06.title: Complementary counting
pumac-2009-team-06.body:
There are $9\cdot10^4=90000$ five-digit numbers (no leading zero). Those with all digits different: $9\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6=27216$. So $n=90000-27216=62784$.

The digit sum of $n$ is $6+2+7+8+4=27$, and $27^2=729$.

**Answer: 729**

pumac-2009-team-07.title: The sequence has period 5
pumac-2009-team-07.body:
Let $x_1=a$, $x_2=b$. Then $x_3=\frac{1+b}{a}$, $x_4=\frac{a+b+1}{ab}$, $x_5=\frac{1+a}{b}$, $x_6=a$, $x_7=b$. So the sequence has period $5$. Since $2009=5\cdot401+4$, $x_{2009}=x_4=\frac{1+a+b}{ab}=\frac{301}{20000}=0.01505$.

The digits after the decimal point are $01505$.

**Answer: 01505**

pumac-2009-team-08.title: Fill positions from the end
pumac-2009-team-08.body:
For $k\ge3$ the condition $s_k\ge k-2$ allows the $12-k$ values $k-2,\ldots,9$. Going down from $k=9$: $s_9$ has $3$ choices ($7,8,9$). When we reach $s_k$, the $9-k$ digits already placed (in positions $9,\ldots,k+1$) all lie in the allowed range $k-2,\ldots,9$, so exactly $12-k-(9-k)=3$ choices remain. This gives $3$ choices for each of $s_9,s_8,\ldots,s_3$ (seven positions).

The remaining three digits go into $s_0,s_1,s_2$, which have no restriction ($k-2\le0$), in $3!=6$ ways.

Total $3^7\cdot6=2187\cdot6=13122$.

**Answer: 13122**

pumac-2009-team-09.title: Integrate over the position of $P$
pumac-2009-team-09.body:
Let $P=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. The rectangle with diagonal $PQ$ lies inside $C$ iff all four corners do. The corners $(\cos\theta,q_y)$ and $(q_x,\sin\theta)$ are inside iff $|q_y|\le|\sin\theta|$ and $|q_x|\le|\cos\theta|$; then $(q_x,q_y)$ is automatically inside. So $Q$ must lie in the rectangle $[-|\cos\theta|,|\cos\theta|]\times[-|\sin\theta|,|\sin\theta|]$ of area $4|\sin\theta\cos\theta|$, and the conditional probability is $\frac{4|\sin\theta\cos\theta|}{\pi}$.

Averaging over $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$: $$\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{4|\sin\theta\cos\theta|}{\pi}\,d\theta=\frac{4}{2\pi^2}\cdot4\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=\frac{4}{2\pi^2}\cdot4\cdot\frac12=\frac4{\pi^2}.$$ Setting $\frac4{\pi^2}=\frac{1000}{k\pi}$ gives $k=250\pi$.

**Answer: $250\pi$**

pumac-2009-team-10.title: Symmetry
pumac-2009-team-10.body:
There are $9!=362880$ arrangements. Swapping Arthur and Erick pairs each arrangement with Arthur ahead of Erick with exactly one with Erick ahead of Arthur, so exactly half of the arrangements qualify: $\frac{9!}{2}=181440$.

**Answer: 181440**

pumac-2009-team-11.title: Expected order statistic
pumac-2009-team-11.body:
The $2009$ numbers split the interval $[0,1]$ into $2010$ gaps, and by symmetry all gaps have the same expected length $\frac1{2010}$. The $456$th largest number is the $2009-456+1=1554$th smallest, so it is the sum of $1554$ gaps, with expectation $\frac{1554}{2010}=\frac{259}{335}$ (in lowest terms). Concatenating: $259335$.

**Answer: 259335**

pumac-2009-team-12.title: Column sums
pumac-2009-team-12.body:
Write $a,b,c$ with four digits each (leading zeros allowed) and let $s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4$ be the sums of the units, tens, hundreds and thousands digits of $a,b,c$ (each between $0$ and $27$). Then $s_1+10s_2+100s_3+1000s_4=2009$ and we want to maximise $s_1+s_2+s_3+s_4$. Since $s_1\equiv9\pmod{10}$, $s_1\in\{9,19\}$; the best is greedy: $s_1=19$, then $s_2+10s_3+100s_4=199$ gives $s_2\in\{9,19\}$, best $s_2=19$, then $s_3+10s_4=18$ gives $(s_3,s_4)=(18,0)$ or $(8,1)$, with totals $56$ and $47$. Comparing all branches the maximum is $M=19+19+18+0=56$, attained only with $(s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4)=(19,19,18,0)$.

Number of digit triples $(d_1,d_2,d_3)$ with each $d_i\in\{0,\ldots,9\}$ and sum $19$: replace $d_i$ by $9-d_i$ to get sum $8$: $\binom{10}2=45$. For sum $18$: the complement sum is $9$: $\binom{11}2=55$. For sum $0$: $1$.

The columns are independent, so there are $45\cdot45\cdot55\cdot1=111375$ triples. (All of $a,b,c$ are positive since each units-digit triple sums to $19>18$.)

**Answer: 111375**

pumac-2009-team-13.title: Ceva and Menelaus
pumac-2009-team-13.body:
The right angle is at $C$, $AC=80$, $AB=100$, so $BC=60$. Then $AQ=60$, $QC=20$, $CP=20$, $PB=40$.

**Ceva** (cevians $AP,BQ,CS$ concurrent at $R$): $\frac{AQ}{QC}\cdot\frac{CP}{PB}\cdot\frac{BS}{SA}=1$, so $3\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac{BS}{SA}=1$ and $\frac{BS}{SA}=\frac23$, i.e. $BS=40$, $SA=60$.

**Menelaus** (line $PQT$ through the triangle $ABC$): $\frac{AQ}{QC}\cdot\frac{CP}{PB}\cdot\frac{BT}{TA}=1$, so $\frac{BT}{TA}=\frac23$ with $T$ beyond $B$ on line $AB$. Then $TA=TB+100$ and $3BT=2(BT+100)$, so $BT=200$.

So $S$ and $T$ are on opposite sides of $B$ and $TS=BT+BS=200+40=240$.

**Answer: 240**

pumac-2009-team-14.title: Find $p$
pumac-2009-team-14.body:
Write $p(x)=c\prod(x-r_i)$ with integer roots $r_i$ and integer leading coefficient $c$. The constant term is $c\prod(-r_i)=-1$, so $c=\pm1$ and every root is $\pm1$. Thus $p(x)=c(x-1)^r(x+1)^s$. From $p(0)=c(-1)^r=-1$ and $p(3)=c\,2^r4^s=2^{r+2s}=128=2^7$ (so $c=1$ and $r$ is odd, since $c\cdot2^{r+2s}>0$), we get $r+2s=7$ with $r$ odd. To minimise the degree $r+s=7-s$ we maximise $s$: $s=3$, $r=1$. So $p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)^3$ and $p(6)=5\cdot7^3=1715$.

In base $3$: $1715=2\cdot729+257$, $257=1\cdot243+14$, $14=1\cdot9+5$, $5=1\cdot3+2$, so $1715=2\cdot3^6+1\cdot3^5+0\cdot3^4+0\cdot3^3+1\cdot3^2+1\cdot3+2$. Hence $p(6)=2100112_3$.

**Answer: 2100112**

pumac-2009-team-15.title: Right triangle
pumac-2009-team-15.body:
$130^2+144^2=16900+20736=37636=194^2$, so the triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse $194$. The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so the circumradius is $97$ and the circumcircle has area $\pi\cdot97^2=9409\pi$.

**Answer: $9409\pi$**

pumac-2009-team-16.title: Use the given information
pumac-2009-team-16.body:
If $1$ and $10$ were on the same side, $n=1001$, and $1001=c^3+d^3$ would need another pair of cubes; but for $c=1,\ldots,9$, $1001-c^3=1000,993,974,937,876,785,658,489,272$, and the only cube is $1000$ (the same pair). So $1$ and $10$ are on different sides: $1+b^3=10^3+d^3$, i.e. $b^3-d^3=999=27\cdot37$.

Write $b-d=t$: $t(t^2+3bd)=999$, i.e. $b^2+bd+d^2=\frac{999}{t}$. For $t=1$: $3d^2+3d+1=999$, no integer solution. For $t=3$: $3d^2+9d+9=333$, $d=9$, $b=12$. For $t=9$: $3d^2+27d+81=111$, $d=1$, $b=10$ (the given pair). Larger divisors $t=27,37,\ldots$ are too large. So $b=12$, $d=9$ and $n=1+12^3=1729=10^3+9^3$.

**Answer: 1729**

pumac-2009-team-17.title: Add up the scores
pumac-2009-team-17.body:
The clue points add up to $(2+4+5+4+5+3+5+5+3)+(3+5+10+5+6+3+4+1)=36+37=73$. The grid has $54$ white squares (counting them row by row).

The maximum score is $73+0.5\cdot54=73+27=100$, and one fourth of it is $25$.

**Answer: 25**
